content.text: This recipe makes 1 litre of
dashi
and takes around 20 minutes. It is the foundational stock of Japanese cooking. You use it in miso soup, ramen broths, simmered dishes, and dipping sauces. The stock gets its depth from
kombu
kelp and
katsuobushi
flakes, which together create a clean, powerful
umami
base.

Do not boil the kombu. Heat it gently and remove it just before the water reaches a full simmer. Boiling kombu makes the stock bitter and slimy. The katsuobushi also needs to steep off the heat. Squeezing the flakes through the sieve clouds the stock and makes it taste harsh. Let gravity do the draining.
What you need

items.prepNote: wiped gently with a damp cloth, do not wash

content.text: Method
Place the kombu in a large saucepan with the cold water. Leave it to soak for at least 20 minutes if you have time. This draws out more flavour.
Set the pan over medium-low heat. Warm the water slowly. Small bubbles will start to appear around the kombu as the water approaches a simmer.
Remove the kombu just before the water reaches a full simmer. You will see small bubbles rising from the base of the pan. This takes around 10 minutes.
Bring the water to a brief boil, then remove the pan from the heat. Add all the katsuobushi flakes at once.
Leave the flakes to steep for 3 to 4 minutes. They will sink gradually to the bottom of the pan.
Line a fine sieve with a piece of muslin or a clean j-cloth. Set it over a large bowl or jug. Pour the stock through the sieve. Do not press the flakes. Allow the stock to drain naturally.
Use the dashi immediately or cool it quickly and store in the fridge for up to 3 days.

items.cause: The kombu was boiled rather than removed before simmering
items.fix: Watch the pot carefully. Remove the kombu as soon as small bubbles form at the base of the pan, before a full rolling boil.

items.cause: The katsuobushi was pressed through the sieve
items.fix: Never squeeze or press the flakes. Let the stock drain by itself through the muslin. A clear dashi takes patience.

items.cause: The kombu did not soak long enough, or the flakes did not steep long enough
items.fix: Soak the kombu for 30 minutes in cold water before heating. Let the katsuobushi steep for the full 4 minutes before straining.

content.text: Where this dish lives

Dashi is made in home kitchens across Japan every single day. It underpins the whole of Japanese cuisine in a way that no single stock does in any other food tradition. This version is called ichiban dashi, meaning first dashi. It is the clearest and most delicate. The spent kombu and flakes can be used again with fresh water to make niban dashi, a second, lighter stock used for simmered dishes.
